# Lead Getters — Get Other People To Get You Leads

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, Section IV "Get Lead Getters" (lines ~2924–4173).
Once you max out the Core Four *on your own*, you scale by getting **other people to do the Core Four
for you**. Those people are **Lead Getters**. This file holds all four. Each sub-skill reads its own
section: `hormozi-lead-referrals` → **## Referrals**, `hormozi-lead-employees` → **## Employees**,
`hormozi-lead-agencies` → **## Agencies**, `hormozi-lead-affiliates` → **## Affiliates**.

---

## Overview — It's All About Leverage

**Leverage = how much you get for the time you spend getting it** (l.2936). Someone with the internet
reaches millions in the time it takes someone with postcards to reach a few — higher leverage. People
learn about your stuff two ways: **you** tell them (Core Four) or **other people** tell them (Core
Four on your behalf). Those other people are **Lead Getters**, and they buy you leverage (l.2942).

### The four leverage scenarios (l.2944–2960)

| Scenario | Setup | Work | Leads | Leverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **#1 — You are the lead getter** | You do the Core Four all day, alone | HIGH | LOW | LOW |
| **#2 — You get a lead getter** | One lead getter does the Core Four for you | LOW | LOW | HIGH |
| **#3 — You get lots of lead getters** | You spend all day getting more lead getters | HIGH | HIGH | HIGHER |
| **#4 — You get a lead getter who gets lead getters** | You recruit one who recruits others; leads climb without you | LOW | HIGH | HIGHEST |

Scenario #4 is the makings of a *$100M Leads* machine.

### The four Lead Getters (l.2974–2980)

Lead Getters aren't part of the Core Four — you don't "do" them, you **get** them (using the Core Four),
and then **they** do the Core Four for you. The Core Four **stacks**: once to get the lead getter, again
when the lead getter gets leads on your behalf — and it repeats (lead getters get lead getters).

1. **Customers** — buy your stuff, then tell others about it (referrals).
2. **Employees** — people inside your business you train to get leads.
3. **Agencies** — service businesses you pay to get leads (and to teach you).
4. **Affiliates** — independent businesses that tell their audience about your stuff.

### Natural order to add them (l.4151–4169)

Their key strengths and the order they tend to appear:

- **Referrals** — biggest potential for low-cost **exponential** growth. *(first, on your own)*
- **Employees** — your **direct** influence; run your business on your behalf. *(as you build a team)*
- **Agencies** — teach you skills you **keep forever** and transfer to your team. *(seeking pro help)*
- **Affiliates** — once going, can operate **entirely on their own**. *(managing people outside your business)*

Expect to **crack a new lead source in three to six months** — losses early are normal; pick one and
stick to it (l.4169).

## Referrals

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, "#1 Customer Referrals – Word of Mouth" (l.2992–3336).
The lowest-cost, highest-profit, best-quality leads there are. *"An amazing product turns every
customer into a lead getter"* (l.3066).

### How referrals work & grow the business (l.3074–3106)

A **referral** = a referrer sends an engaged lead to your business. Anyone can refer; the **best come
from customers**. Referrals grow the business two ways:

1. **Worth more (higher LTGP)** — they buy more expensive stuff, more often, and tend to pay cash
   upfront.
2. **Cost less (lower CAC)** — a referred customer costs you nothing.

*Illustration (l.3088):* at a 4:1 LTGP:CAC you spend 25% of one customer's lifetime gross profit to get
the next. If **every customer brought two more**, you'd be at **12:1** (8.3%) — three customers for the
price of one. And referrals are **exponential**, not linear: one brings two, two bring four, four bring
eight.

**Referral growth equation (l.3094–3100):** Referrals (in) − churned customers (out).
- Referrals **>** churn → you grow with no other advertising.
- Referrals **=** churn → you need other advertising to grow.
- Referrals **<** churn → you advertise just to break even (where most businesses sit).

### Two reasons most businesses don't get referrals (l.3108–3110)

1. **The product isn't as good as they think.**
2. **They don't ask.**

**On the product (l.3124–3130):** Price is what you charge; value is what they get; the difference is
**goodwill** (economists' "customer surplus"). Goodwill → word of mouth → referrals. Two ways to build
goodwill: lower price (temporary, "any fool can sell something for less") or **give more value** — so
the real question is *how do we give more value?*

### Six Ways To Get More Referrals By Giving More Value (l.3132–3232)

These map to the parts of an ad. Run all six to build goodwill.

**1. Call Outs → Sell Better Customers (l.3148–3156).** Better customers get the most value → most
goodwill → most referrals. *Action:* find what your most successful customers have in common; target a
new audience matching those traits; sell only people who meet the new criteria.

**2. Dream Outcome → Set Better Expectations (l.3158–3164).** Cheapest way to be remarkable: beat their
expectations — and *you* set the expectations, so lower them to leave room to overdeliver. *Action:*
slowly lower the promises you make in offers until your close rates start to drop, then stop.

**3. Increase Perceived Likelihood of Achievement → Get More People Better Results (l.3166–3186).**
Find what your best-result customers do; make everyone do it. *(Gym Launch: owners who ran ads + made a
sale in the first 7 days tripled their LTGP → they forced everyone to do that.)* Six steps:
1. **Survey** customers to find the ones with the best results.
2. **Interview** them to find what they did differently.
3. Look at the **actions** they had in common.
4. **Force** new customers to repeat those actions.
5. **Measure** the improvement in average results (speed and outcome).
6. **Match your guarantee's conditions** to the actions that produce the best results.

**4. Decrease Time Delay → Make Faster Wins (l.3188–3206).** A "win" = any positive experience. Give
wins **more often** to make them feel faster (raises perceived speed, retention, trust). Five ways:
1. Deliver several small things at **shorter intervals**, not all at once.
2. **Updates are wins** — share progress as often as possible.
3. Customers form a lasting impression in the **first 48 hours** — force wins in that window.
4. They should always know the next time they'll hear from you — **BAMFAM: Book-A-Meeting-From-A-Meeting.**
5. **Deliver early, never late** — add 50% to your timelines so "on time" for you is early for them.

**5. Decrease Effort & Sacrifice → Keep Making Your Stuff Better (l.3208–3222).** Run monthly:
1. Use customer-service data, surveys, and reviews to find the **most common problem**.
2. Figure out the fix — get input from customers who succeeded *despite* the problem.
3. Use that feedback to **improve** the product.
4. Give the new version to a **small group** of struggling customers.
5. Get the next round of feedback — solved → roll out to all; not solved → back to step 2.
6. Move to the next most common problem and repeat.

**6. Call To Action → Tell Them What To Buy Next (l.3224–3232).** A great product makes them want more
— satisfy it or they buy from someone else. Sell them again (a new thing or more of the same); more
things to buy = more to refer. *Action:* treat every customer like a first-time sale; make the next
offer more compelling than the first; remind them to buy after each big win.

**One Question to Rule Them All (l.3234–3246):** *You've lost every customer but one, and all future
customers must come from that one.* How would you treat them? What results, onboarding, and customer
type would make them refer everyone they know? Write it out — then do it.

### Ask For Them — treat the ask like an offer (l.3250–3260)

Most businesses under-refer because **they never ask**. Asking only works when you **treat it like an
offer** — show the value the customer gets by referring. *Dropbox: free storage to customer AND friend
→ 39x'd in 15 months. PayPal: $10 credit to customer AND friend → 1M users in 2 years, 100M in 6.*

**Seven Ways To Ask For Referrals (l.3262–3306).** Three components to any referral program: *how you
give the incentive, what you incentivize with, and how you ask.* The seven proven combos:

1. **One-Sided Referral Benefit** — pay your average CAC to the referrer *or* the friend. *(e.g. CAC
   $200: ask for a real 3-way intro via call/SMS/email right when they buy, then $200 check when the
   friend signs up OR $200 off for the friend.)* Great for spouses — ask for the spouse, give a
   household discount.
2. **Two-Sided Referral Benefits** — Dropbox/PayPal model: split your CAC across both. *(e.g. $500
   program, $200 CAC → $100 cash to referrer + $100 off for the friend, up to 3 friends.)*
3. **Ask Right When They Buy** — on the contract/checkout, ask for names & numbers of people they'd
   like to do this *with*; show they get better results with a friend. *Script:* "People who do our
   program with someone else tend to get 3x the results. Who else could you do this program with?"
4. **Referrals As A Negotiation Chip** — trade a discount for intros. *"I can't go below $500 down, but
   if you make a 3-way text intro to a few friends right now, I'd cut the initiation fee."* (If a
   full-price customer objects, offer them the same deal for three friends.)
5. **Referral Events** — points/credits/dollars/bragging rights for bringing friends within a set
   window (1–4 weeks). Names: "Bring-a-Friend," "Spouse Challenge," "Accountability Buddy," "Coach
   Challenge."
6. **Ongoing Referral Programs** — talk up doing-it-with-others *all the time* (content, outreach, ads).
   *(A buddy saw a 33% boost in total sign-ups; 250k of 1M event-ticket buyers were referred.)*
7. **Unlockable Referral Bonuses** — bonuses for people who (1) refer and (2) leave a testimonial:
   VIP bonuses, courses, tokens, status, training, merch, service levels, premium support, extra hours.
   Good when you'd rather not pay cash.

### Referral program mechanics — worked combo (l.3310–3318)

Give every customer a **gift card for one-third the cost of their program**, usable only if a friend
signs up with them; **expire it in 7–14 days** to force use. It gives the referrer *status* ("I got
this $2,000 card, want it? I don't want to waste it"). Optionally sell the gift cards at **90% off** as
purchasable gifts (only for friends of customers).

**Referrals are a *way of doing business*, not a hack (l.3320–3332).** Referring risks the customer's
goodwill with their friend, so they only refer when a good experience is very likely. *Action Items:*
baseline your referral % and churn %; run the six value steps to build goodwill; then capitalize with
one or more of the seven asks.

## Employees

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, "#2 Employees" (l.3338–3556). Hormozi calls it the most valuable chapter.

### How employees work & why they make you wealthy (l.3384–3408)

**Lead-getting employees** are people you train to get you leads the same way you did (run ads, make &
post content, do outreach). More of them = more engaged leads + **less work for you**. They take work,
but far less than doing it yourself: trade **40 hours of doing for 4 hours of managing** → 36 hours
saved, and you can make that trade over and over (l.3388).

**Why wealthy, not just rich (l.3392–3408):** a business that makes $5M rev / $2M profit but only runs
*with you* is a high-paying job and a bad investment for anyone else. The **same** business running
*without you* becomes a sellable **asset** — that $2M/yr profit could be worth **$10M+**. The mindset
shift is the whole chapter: *"You get rich from what you make. You become wealthy from what you own."*
New beliefs about talent (l.3430–3434): *if you want it done right, get someone to spend all their time
doing it; if I can do it, someone else can do it better; everyone is replaceable, especially me.*

### The Internal Core Four — get employees the same way you get customers (l.3438–3456)

Reframe "let **customers** know about your stuff" → "let **employees** know about your stuff." Same
activities:

| Getting customers | → Getting employees |
|---|---|
| Warm Outreach | Asking Your Network |
| Cold Outreach | Recruiting |
| Post Content | Posting Job Openings |
| Paid Ads | Promoting Job Postings |
| Customer Referrals | Employee Referrals |
| Affiliates | Associations, Guilds, Listservs, etc. |
| Agencies | Staffing firms, etc. |
| Employees | Employees (unchanged) |

### How to get employees to get you leads — the 3 Ds (l.3458–3474)

Train them with the **3 Ds mental model: Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate.**

1. **Document — you make a checklist.** Write the steps exactly as you do them (record yourself doing it
   multiple ways/shifts so you observe without breaking flow). Test: can *you* do an A+ job following
   *only* your written directions? If yes, you have draft one.
2. **Demonstrate — you do it in front of them.** Walk them through the checklist step by step. Every
   time they stop or slow you to understand something, **fix the checklist** → draft two.
3. **Duplicate — they do it in front of you.** They follow the same checklist while you observe. If the
   checklist is right, the outcome matches; where it's off, you find out fast. Fix until it's right,
   then have them run it until they nail it.

**Training rules (l.3476–3494):**
- If they get it wrong or confused, **you** got it wrong / made it confusing (a step that needs
  explaining is too complicated or is really several steps).
- **Competence ≠ performance** — they can know the steps and still need reps ("slow, then smooth, then
  fast"). Don't change the checklist; give practice.
- Focus on their **ability to follow directions** over the result — if they follow exactly and get the
  wrong result, *it's the directions* (which you control). Praise them anyway, then fix the checklist.
- **Reward, don't punish**, during training; give one piece of feedback at a time.
- On a major dip in performance, **retrain** — a key step got dropped.

### Calculating returns from lead-getting employees (l.3496–3532)

Excluding paid-ad spend, employee advertising cost ≈ payroll. Compare payroll to the leads it produces:

- **Total Payroll ÷ Total Engaged Leads = cost per engaged lead** *(e.g. $100,000 / 1,000 = $100/lead)*.
- 1-in-10 leads convert → **CAC = $100 × 10 = $1,000**.
- LTGP $4,000 → **LTGP:CAC = 4:1**.
- *(Acquisition.com: ~30,000 engaged leads/mo from a ~$100k/mo content team = **$3.33/lead**, no ads,
  no outreach.)*

**Which employees to focus on (l.3514–3532).** If CAC is within **3x** industry average, you're good
enough — focus on raising LTGP. If CAC is **more than 3x** industry average, diagnose with one question:
> *"Do my engaged leads have the problem I solve and the money to spend?"*
- **No** → not qualified → **advertising problem.**
- **Yes**, but not enough of them buying → **advertising problem.**
- **Yes**, qualified but not buying → **sales problem.**

Don't fire the sales rep for an advertising problem, or advertising staff for a sales problem.
*(For low-level roles, labor is never scarce — who you pick matters less than how you train them.)*

## Agencies

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, "#3 Agencies" (l.3577–3762). The non-obvious, much-better way to use them.

### How agencies really work (l.3621–3653)

Agencies are **lead-getting service businesses** — you pay them to run paid ads, do outreach, or
package/distribute content. The trap Hormozi hit 10+ times (l.3629–3649): (1) excited about new leads →
(2) valuable-feeling onboarding → (3) their "best" **senior rep** on your account → (4) some results →
(5) senior rep moved to the newest client → (6) a **junior rep** takes over, results suffer → (7) you
complain → (8) senior rep pops back briefly → (9) results still suffer, you cancel → (10) find another
agency → (11) wonder why it's never like the first time. Agencies *can* add value — **but not the way
they want you to.** The chapter's three parts: (1) hire vs DIY, (2) how to use them now, (3) how to pick.

### 1. Hire an agency vs do it yourself (l.3661–3671)

Good agencies **cost money** — no money → agencies are out, learn by trial and error. If you *have*
money, use agencies for **exactly two things**: **learning new methods** and **learning new
platforms.** They've already made the big mistakes; you skip to the "make money" part and avoid burning
the time/attention needed to scale. *Action:* as soon as you can afford a good agency, start poking
around.

### 2. How to use agencies now — learn, then leave (l.3673–3691)

Start every relationship with a **purpose and a deadline**. Open with this template (l.3677):
> *"I want to do what you do in my business, but I don't know how. I'd like to work with you for 6
> months to learn how you do it. I'll pay extra for you to break down why you make the decisions you
> do. Then I'll train my team, and once they're good enough, move to a lower-cost consulting
> arrangement so you can still help. Are you opposed to this?"*

- Most agencies aren't opposed; if one is, move on — **be willing to negotiate** (at some price it's
  worth it for both).
- Proven variant: hire one **"good enough"** agency to learn a new platform, then a more **elite**
  agency (Hormozi paid 4x) to learn to maximize it.
- You get a **fraction** of an agency's attention (worse as they add clients) while **your team** only
  gets better. **Compare your team's results to the agency's; once yours wins, cancel** and pour the
  money into scaling what you learned.

### 3. How to pick the right agency — the 10-point checklist (l.3693–3727)

1. **Someone you know** got good results with them. *(Word-of-mouth agencies beat those you only found
   via their own ads/outreach.)*
2. **Prominent companies** you recognize got good results with them.
3. **A waiting list** (demand exceeds supply).
4. A **clear sales process** that sets realistic expectations — no funny business.
5. **No short-term hacks** — long-term strategy, with clear timelines for setup, scaling, results.
6. They tell you **exactly what they need from you, when, and how** they use it.
7. **They** propose a regular meeting schedule and several ways to update you.
8. Updates in **simple terms**, with clear tracking so you can compare cost vs results.
9. **They make a good offer** — judged on the four value elements:
   a. **Dream outcome** — is what they promise what you want?
   b. **Perceived likelihood** — how many others like you have they gotten there?
   c. **Time delay** — how long will it take?
   d. **Effort & sacrifice** — what will they require of you / what must you give up, and can you
      sustain it?
10. **They are expensive.** All good agencies are expensive — but not all expensive agencies are good.

Even if an agency agrees to your terms, **talk to a few more** before deciding.

### Next steps (l.3741–3753)

1. Decide if an agency makes sense right now. 2. Talk to **a lot** of agencies — don't be cheap.
3. Use the agreement template. 4. Set a clear **deadline** to force you and your team to learn.
5. Run both teams until yours **beats theirs** regularly. 6. Drop to discounted consulting until you're
teaching them, then cut them loose. *(Hormozi now gets his team as good/better than an agency in **≤6
months**; the opening story cost 8 hours + $6,000 for a skill that made him millions.)*

## Affiliates

**Source:** *$100M Leads*, "#4 Affiliates and Partners" (l.3765–4146). The lead getter that made
Hormozi the most money; ALAN + Prestige Labs did **$75M+** from **5,000+** affiliates.

### How affiliates work (l.3799–3803)

An **affiliate** is a lead getter: an **independent business** that tells *their* audience to buy *your*
stuff. Unlike referrers, they run their **own** business and their **own** advertising, and they agree
to offer your stuff to their engaged leads in exchange for **money, free stuff, or both**. You get them
by advertising and making them an **offer just like a customer** — but a *unique* one: instead of
offering your product, you offer **a fast, simple, easy way to make commissions promoting it.**

### Why you want an affiliate army (l.3805–3829)

Each affiliate is another **stream** of leads. Same effort, wildly different ceilings:
- **Selling 10 customers/mo** at $10k → caps at $100k/mo → $1.2M/yr, then plateaus. *Low leverage.*
- **Selling 10 affiliates/mo**, each bringing one $10k customer/mo → **adds $100k every month** →
  **$7.8M** in 12 months, and it keeps growing. *High leverage.*
*(ALAN's 3 affiliate levels compounded to $1.7M/mo within six months of launch.)*

### How To Build An Affiliate Army in Six Steps (l.3831–4049)

> Step 1 Find Ideal Affiliates → Step 2 Make Them an Offer → Step 3 Qualify Them → Step 4 Figure Out
> What To Pay Them → Step 5 Get Them Advertising (Launch) → Step 6 Keep Them Advertising (Integrate)

**Step 1 — Find Your Ideal Affiliate (l.3853–3873).** The ideal affiliate has a business with a **warm
audience full of people like your customers.** Build the "hit list" by asking about your best
customers: *What do they buy? → who provides it. Where do they go? → what businesses surround those
places. What do they like to do? → who provides those services.* (DTC: what businesses employ your
consumers?) In a nutshell: **"Who's got my leads?"** Sort candidates into six categories: **softwares,
products, equipment, services, groups they belong to, events they attend** — a business in *multiple*
categories is an especially strong affiliate.

**Step 2 — Make Them An Offer (l.3875–3903).** Advertise the affiliate offer like any offer — call out,
show value, call to action — but the value you sell is **a new way to make money.**
- **Call outs** target: the affiliate owners themselves; the affiliate's customers; results the
  affiliate promises; products/services the affiliate delivers; or your own customers ("know anyone who
  owns a spa?").
- **Elements of value** template (l.3899): *make more money from your current customers + get more leads
  than your current offer (dream outcome)… with a high chance of working since your customers already
  want it (perceived likelihood)… without building, delivering, or supporting the product yourself
  (effort & sacrifice)… so you can start selling tomorrow (time delay).*

**Step 3 — Qualify Them (l.3905–3919).** They become real affiliates when they **understand and agree
to your terms** — set terms that force a fast first win by getting them to **invest** (time, money, and
in the product): *"if they pay, they'll pay attention."* Two ways (use either or both):
- **Way #1 — Make Them A Customer:** they must buy (and ideally use) the product to keep affiliate
  status. Lowest barrier; more they invest, more they earn.
- **Way #2 — Make Them An Expert:** they pay for onboarding/training that **certifies** them (can be
  credited from the product they bought). Covers your advertising cost and funds proper onboarding of
  every affiliate.
- **How much to charge:** **10–20% of what the average active affiliate makes in their first 12
  months.** *(Avg affiliate earns $40k/yr → charge $4,000–$8,000.)* Too low → no investment; too high →
  too few affiliates. If unsure, raise the minimum every 5 sign-ups until you hit the sweet spot.

**Step 4 — Figure Out What To Pay Them (l.3921–3967).** Two questions: **what** they get paid for and
**how much.**
- **What they get paid for:** first decide *exactly what you want the affiliate to do*, then pay for
  that. Default: **new customers and repeat customers**; over time, pay for pre-customer steps you know
  convert (lead magnets downloaded, appointments set).
- **How much:** base it on your **maximum allowable CAC.** *(Product sells $200, costs $40 to fulfill →
  $160 to split; at 3:1 LTGP:CAC, $120 to the business and $40 max to the affiliate.)*
- **Three-tier payout structure** (with a $40 max CAC):
  - **Tier 1 — 25% CAC = $10:** anyone who agrees to initial terms (signs up / buys product or cert).
  - **Tier 2 — 50% CAC = $20:** once they **activate** (finish the certification, hit a post/outreach
    count, run a launch) — double pay rewards activation.
  - **Tier 3 — 100% CAC = $40:** once they **sustain** performance (e.g. maintain 5 subscription
    customers/mo).
  - **Hidden benefit:** blended payout is **less** than max CAC. *(20% Tier1 / 20% Tier2 / 60% Tier3 →
    blended $30, so 3:1 becomes 4:1;* leftover funds contests, recruiting, rising stars.)

**Step 5 — Get Them Advertising = Launch (l.3969–4005).** Treat affiliates like customers — give them
something good, fast: **launches and cash**. Affiliates advertise your lead magnet / core offer to
their audience *before* it's buyable, then sell at launch. Do the work for them so they can plug and
play, using the **Whisper–Tease–Shout** method:
- **Whisper (think "Call Outs"):** build **curiosity**; keep the product mysterious, hint it's a big
  deal, show behind-the-scenes; can start years out. *Cadence:* whisper every **4–6 weeks until 60 days
  out**, then every **2–3 weeks until 30 days out.**
- **Tease (think "Elements of Value"):** start satisfying the curiosity — reveal the product, make the
  date public, show value using the **What-Who-When** framework. *Cadence:* **once/week until 14 days
  out**, then **twice/week until 3 days out.**
- **Shout (think "Call to Action"):** specific actions to take at launch — bonuses, scarcity, urgency,
  "be first" guarantees. *Cadence:* **≥2x/day from 3 days out**; on launch day every few hours until 2
  hours out, then **every 30 minutes** until you launch.

**Step 6 — Keep Them Advertising = Integrate (l.4007–4049).** Selling once and getting leads for life
comes from **integration** — three ways to embed your product into their offer, easiest → hardest:
1. **Affiliates give your lead magnet away** when someone buys their stuff (makes their offer more
   valuable, lets them charge more, feeds you leads). Forms: a **sample/trial** (free massage), a
   **problem-reveal** (free posture assessment), or **one step of a multi-step process** — you upsell
   from there. *(Hormozi: gyms gave a free nutrition consult, then upsold products.)*
2. **Affiliates sell your lead magnet** (book, event, service, software, sample) — often keeping all the
   cash (all profit / no work for them); you profit on the core offer they feed you. *(Gyms sold a
   $99–$199 nutrition consult, kept the money, then Hormozi upsold products.)*
3. **Affiliates sell your core offer** directly — they earn a higher % of your LTGP; you just deliver.
   *(Split upfront cash, all cash for a period, or all cash forever — Hormozi prefers paying **forever**
   and **never caps payouts**.)*
   *(Hormozi runs Strategy 1 twice/year as a big event + Strategy 3 ongoing; many portfolio cos use 2.)*

### Costs and returns (l.4083–4130)

Affiliates invert the math: you spend to *get* the affiliate, but the money comes back **from the
customers they bring** — so compare **cost-to-get-an-affiliate** vs **gross profit of all customers they
send.** Worked example:

- CAC to get an affiliate = **$4,000**.
- Affiliate sells $10,000/mo, stays 12 mo → **$120,000** total sales.
- 75% gross margin (25% COGS = $30,000) → **$90,000** gross profit.
- Pay affiliate **40%** of gross profit → **$36,000**.
- Leftover: $120,000 − $30,000 − $36,000 = **$54,000**.
- **Affiliate LTGP:CAC = $54,000 / $4,000 = 12.5:1.**

Need **≥3:1**; aim higher (5:1, 10:1+). If below 3:1, three fixes (l.4121):
1. **Lower CAC** — get affiliates for less (better ads, offer, sales process).
2. **Increase LTGP & decrease CAC** — get more to **activate** (build a launch process).
3. **Increase LTGP** — make them **worth more** (improve integration).

*Action (l.4143):* advertise the affiliate offer until you land **10–20 affiliates**; get results, work
out the kinks in offer/terms/launch/integration; then scale by turning their results into your first
batch of affiliate lead magnets.
